lesson.title: How Many Do You Have? len on Lists
lesson.summary: The same len() function you used to measure string length also reports how many elements a list contains, and it does so instantly no matter how long the list is.
lesson.body:
You have already met len when measuring strings, where len('hello') returns 5, the number of characters. len is not actually a string-only tool. It is a general-purpose function that works on any sequence, and a list is a sequence, so len(mylist) returns the number of elements the list holds.

```python
inventory = ['sword', 'shield', 'potion']
print(len(inventory))

empty = []
print(len(empty))
```

This prints 3, the count of items in inventory, and then 0, because an empty list has no elements at all. len is one of the most frequently used functions in this entire course, because it shows up everywhere lists do: as the upper bound in a range-based for loop, such as for i in range(len(mylist)), as the divisor when computing an average with sum(mylist) / len(mylist), and as a simple sanity check that a list was built the size you expected.

One detail worth knowing, even though it rarely changes how you write code: len on a list is fast no matter how big the list is. Python lists keep track of their own length as a stored property of the list object itself, updating it automatically every time you append, insert, or remove an element, so calling len does not need to walk through and count every element by hand. This is different from, say, counting how many times a value appears with count, which genuinely does have to look at every element. In practice this means you should never hesitate to call len inside a loop condition out of a worry that it is slow: checking len(mylist) is essentially instant, regardless of whether the list holds five elements or five million.
